title: Tokens: what they are and what they cost
summary: BPE is a compression algorithm repurposed as a tokenizer, and the 4 chars per token rule breaks badly on code and non-Latin scripts. Tokenizers are model specific, and query-side context, not indexing, is what actually dominates a RAG bill.
html:
Every number so far has been in words, because words are easy to reason about. Nothing in the stack actually counts words. Models read, charge, and truncate in tokens, and the mapping from one to the other is lumpy enough that getting it wrong shows up on a bill.

What a tokenizer actually does

Byte Pair Encoding is the algorithm behind most of them, and it is much simpler than its reputation. Training it:

  1. Start with a vocabulary of individual characters. Every word is a sequence of them.
  2. Count every adjacent pair across the corpus. Find the most frequent.
  3. Merge that pair into a single new symbol and add it to the vocabulary.
  4. Repeat until the vocabulary hits a target size, usually 30k to 200k.

Run it on English and the early merges are the obvious ones. t plus h becomes th. Then th plus e becomes the. Common words get absorbed whole, so they cost one token each. Rare words never get merged fully and stay as fragments.

This is a compression algorithm, and it was one first. BPE comes from a 1994 data compression paper and was repurposed for tokenization in 2015. If you have implemented a dictionary coder, you have implemented most of BPE.

Why subword, and not something simpler

The choice is a classic tradeoff and it helps to see both ends:

UnitVocabularySequence lengthUnknown words
Characters~100, tinyVery longImpossible, everything is representable
WordsMillions, unboundedShortConstant problem, every typo is out of vocabulary
Subword (BPE)30k to 200kModerateImpossible, falls back to fragments

Subword gets a bounded vocabulary and still represents anything you throw at it, including a hostname you invented this morning. It just spends more tokens doing it.

The exchange rate, and where it breaks

The rule of thumb is about 4 characters per token for English prose. It is a real average and it is unreliable the moment your text is not English prose:

English prose     ~4.0 chars/token    1000 chars = ~250 tokens
code              ~3.0 chars/token    1000 chars = ~333 tokens
non-Latin script  ~1.5 chars/token    1000 chars = ~667 tokens

Code is worse because identifiers, indentation and punctuation do not merge well. getUserByID is one concept and several tokens. Non-Latin scripts are worse again, because the tokenizer's merges were learned on a corpus that was mostly English, so scripts that were rare in training get encoded closer to byte by byte. The practical consequence is that the same document in Hindi or Japanese can cost two to three times more to process than its English translation. That is a real fairness problem in the field, and it is not solved, just reduced with each generation of tokenizer.

The mistake that costs money

Tokenizers are model family specific. There is no universal token.

The most common version of this error is reaching for tiktoken, which is OpenAI's tokenizer, and using it to size prompts for a different vendor's model. Against Claude it undercounts by roughly 15 to 20 percent on ordinary text, and by more on code:

tiktoken says  10,000  ->  actually ~11,500 to 12,000
tiktoken says 100,000  ->  actually ~115,000 to 120,000

Budget a prompt at 100k on a tiktoken estimate and you may be shipping 120k. You find out when something truncates or a bill arrives. Use the provider's own counter: Anthropic exposes a count_tokens endpoint, and it is stateless and cheap, so you can call it on a file or a whole prompt. Other providers ship their own. Never mix them, and never assume an estimate transfers.

The cost model, in tokens

Day 1 gave you two clocks. Now put numbers on them. Take a corpus of a million chunks at 400 tokens each, serving ten thousand queries a day, retrieving five chunks per query:

embed the corpus, once per reindex:   400,000,000 tokens
one query (200 system + 5x400 + 30):        2,230 tokens
one day at 10,000 queries:             22,300,000 tokens

Query-side input passes the cost of embedding the entire corpus in about 18 days. Over a year it is roughly 20 times a full reindex.

That inverts the intuition most people start with. Indexing feels like the expensive part because it is the part that takes hours and that you watch. It is the cheap part. The recurring spend is the context you attach to every single query, and it scales with queries x k x chunk_size, which is exactly the three knobs you have been tuning since Day 6. Raising k from 5 to 10 doubles your largest ongoing bill.

Output tokens are priced higher than input, currently five times higher across Anthropic's lineup, so check current rates rather than trusting a number in a lesson. But RAG is an input-heavy workload: you send thousands of tokens of context to get back a few hundred. Your bill is dominated by what you send, not what you receive.

Caching, and what it does not cover

Prompt caching lets a provider keep a prefix of your request warm, so repeated requests that share it pay much less for that part. It is a prefix match, so any byte that changes invalidates everything after it, and there is a minimum cacheable length (on Anthropic's API, in the range of 512 to 4096 tokens depending on model) below which nothing caches at all.

Here is the part people get wrong. Caching helps your system prompt and your fixed few-shot examples, because those are identical on every request. It does not help your retrieved chunks, because those are different for every question. The largest, most variable part of a RAG prompt is exactly the part caching cannot touch.

There is one important exception where caching completely changes the economics of a technique, and that is contextual retrieval on Day 45. It works by holding a whole document in cache while processing each of its chunks. That is an indexing-time trick, not a query-time one, which is precisely why it works.

Phase 1 has given you chunking, weighting, scoring and now counting. Tomorrow you assemble all of it: your first end-to-end RAG in 100 lines, built only from pieces you have written yourself.
exercise:
1. Measure your own exchange rate. Take three files: a prose document, a source file, and if you have one, something in a non-Latin script. Get a real token count for each from a provider's counting endpoint, divide characters by tokens, and compare against 4.0. Write the three numbers down. That is your corpus's actual exchange rate, and estimating from word counts will be wrong by whatever gap you just measured.

2. Convert Day 6 into tokens. You picked a chunk size in words. Using your measured ratio, what is it in tokens? If you were feeding it to a model with an 8192 token input limit, how many chunks fit alongside a 200 token system prompt and the question? That number is your real ceiling on k.

3. Do the 18 day arithmetic for yourself. Plug in your own corpus size, chunk size, query volume and k. How many days until query-side tokens exceed one full reindex? Then double k and run it again. The point is not the number, it is seeing which of the two clocks your system actually lives on.
